documents: Eastoe and Beisner 2022, Journal of Contemporary Water Research & Education 175: 1-14 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: In this study, the isotope data are reviewed with the aim of providing information about the water resources of the Tucson Mountains

steps.action: Pose the question of the sources and ages of groundwater in and near the Tucson Mountains block and the nature of the aquifer, motivated by falling well levels and drought.
steps.quote: [...] sources and ages of the groundwater in and near the mountain block, and the nature of the aquifer or aquifers

steps.action: Take up the first author's earlier interpretation (Eastoe and Wright 2019) that the unusual hard-rock isotope array is a mixture of younger and older recharge.
steps.quote: the authors suggested that it represents mixing of younger and older recharge

steps.action: Compile groundwater isotope data (stable O, H, S, C isotopes, tritium, 14C) from domestic wells and one spring, measured by IRMS, AMS, gas-proportional and liquid scintillation counting. The compilation combines published datasets with unpublished alluvium data and new mineral δ34S measurements.
steps.quote: Groundwater samples were collected from domestic supply wells in continual use.

steps.action: Compare hard-rock δ18O-δ2H data with the GMWL and local meteoric water lines. The data form a slope-8 array distinct from both, while flanking alluvium plots on a modified LMWL.
steps.quote: form a linear array with a slope near 8, distinct from and to the right of the global meteoric water line

steps.action: Add the independent Old Yuma Mine (area Y) dataset of Beisner and Gray (2018) and check that it conforms to the same mixing array.
steps.quote: Gray (2018) for area Y confirms that conclusion

steps.action: Match the short-residence end member to a modified LMWL for the wettest ~30% of months, adjusted for altitude with lapse rates, and estimate the summer contribution to recharge.
steps.quote: the contributions of summer precipitation are about 50 to 75%

steps.action: Compare tritium and 14C with bomb-pulse thresholds to identify sites with post-1953 recharge. These sites are related to aquifer lithology, with the caveat that examples are few.
steps.quote: occurs at sites that have received recharge since 1953

steps.action: Reject the revised Fontes-Garnier 14C age correction used by Beisner and Gray (2018) for mixed waters, because mixing ratios are unknown and the equations ignore mixing.
steps.quote: the correction equations are not constructed to account for mixing

steps.action: Take from the literature the end-Pleistocene rise in precipitation δ18O, dated in southern Arizona by a Santa Rita Mountains speleothem record.
steps.quote: the shift occurred between 13,000 and 15,000 years ago, on the basis of a speleothem δ18O record

steps.action: Infer a minimum residence time for the low-δ18O end member from its pre-shift isotope signature.
steps.quote: The residence time of the low-δ18O end member is therefore more than 13,000 years.

steps.action: Check the oldest sample (site 6, 8 pMC) against the evaporation trend defined by ancient groundwater (<10 pMC) from other regional studies.
steps.quote: falls on a broad evaporation trend (Figure 2B) defined by other ancient groundwater

steps.action: Infer ages of flanking alluvium groundwater: some post-1953 recharge, much thousands of years old, and no low-δ18O end member.
steps.quote: there is no evidence for recharge older than 13,000 years in the alluvium

steps.action: State rival models of the hard-rock aquifer: porous strata, connected fractures, or unconnected fractures.
steps.quote: may reside in one or more porous strata, or in fractures with or without hydrologic connection

steps.action: Compare isotopically distinct waters in wells ~100 m apart in area S against the rivals and favour a poorly connected fracture system.
steps.quote: consistent with an aquifer or aquifers consisting of a poorly-connected system of fractures

steps.action: Infer local mountain-block (subsurface) recharge into alluvium at sites 31 and 33 from hard-rock-like isotopes and low pMC, and mountain-front recharge elsewhere.
steps.quote: Mountain-block (i.e., subsurface) recharge into alluvium is indicated near these sites.

steps.action: Compare groundwater δ34S with reference ranges for rain, dust, gypsum and ore minerals to attribute poor water quality. Low values are attributed to sulfide oxidation and +14‰ to bacterial sulfate reduction.
steps.quote: probably contains a mixture of rain and dust sulfate with sulfate from oxidation of ore sulfide

steps.action: Keep the account: mixed-age recharge in poorly connected fractures, little present recharge except in Oligocene volcanics and Cretaceous sediments, and a limited supply of variable quality.
steps.quote: Groundwater in fractured-rock aquifers in the Tucson Mountains is a mixture of recharge of different ages.

No; ages, sources and aquifer structure are inferred from isotope tracers
Sources, ages and aquifer nature, for water supply

Conditions found: past recharge read from existing wells

tree.answer: Multiple wells and clusters repeat the mixing pattern
Added area Y dataset conforms to the mixing array
Kept as best explanation; mixed-age recharge in poorly connected fractures
Two anonymous reviewers thanked; no review record supplied

end.claim: Tucson Mountains groundwater is a mixture of late-Pleistocene (>13 ka) and younger wettest-month recharge held in poorly connected fractures that receive little present recharge, so supply is limited and of variable quality.

decisive_move.sentence: Reading the low-δ18O end member as pre-13 ka recharge from the end-Pleistocene isotope shift, instead of from corrected 14C ages, gives the old-water component on which the limited-supply claim rests.

gates.evidence: Data were compiled from wells sampled 1990-2016 for other purposes; area Y was sampled to trace mine contamination (p. 2). The added area Y data could have departed from the inherited mixing array but did not (p. 8). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Gas-proportional and liquid scintillation counting of tritium and 14C
Bomb-pulse tritium and 14C as markers of post-1953 recharge

novelty_claims.quote: previously unpublished data for groundwater from the alluvium flanking the Tucson Mountains are also included in Table 1
three new measurements of δ34S (+0.5, +0.6, and +1.4 ‰, on pyrite and sulfate crust from the base of a waste pile)

limits: No review file was supplied. The paper is mainly a re-analysis of published datasets plus a few unpublished alluvium and mineral analyses. Samples span 1990-2016 and two laboratories, and no inter-laboratory comparison is reported. Sub-claims at other statuses: the residence time of the old end member is a lower bound only (estimate_with_resolution, no stated uncertainty); the summer contribution of 50-75% is an estimate_with_resolution without a stated method of uncertainty; lithologic control of post-bomb recharge is tentative ('The number of examples is small'), so it is at most best_explanation; mountain-block recharge at sites 31 and 33 is best_explanation from two sites. The δ13C mixing interpretation (p. 6) is a minor inference not coded as a step. Inference: sampling followed well access, not a stated hypothesis. The poorly connected fracture conclusion rests on juxtaposed compositions; no hydraulic tests are reported.

disagreements.target: Beisner and Gray (2018) corrected 14C ages using the revised Fontes-Garnier method (Han and Plummer 2013)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that unknown mixing ratios and correction equations that ignore mixing make the corrected ages unreliable. They constrain the residence time instead from the end-Pleistocene δ18O shift.
disagreements.quote: corrections of 14C data using δ13C as an indicator of dissolution of rock carbonate are problematic where mixing contributes to observed isotope compositions

alternatives_considered.chosen: Residence time from the end-Pleistocene δ18O shift (speleothem-dated 13-15 ka)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 14C ages corrected by the revised Fontes-Garnier method
alternatives_considered.reason: Mixing ratios not accurately known; correction equations not constructed for mixing

alternatives_considered.chosen: Modified LMWL from precipitation in the wettest ~30% of months
alternatives_considered.alternatives: LMWL from amount-weighted seasonal mean precipitation for all months
alternatives_considered.reason: Short-residence groundwater matches it, as in neighbouring basins

alternatives_considered.chosen: Mountain-block recharge at sites 31 and 33; mountain-front recharge elsewhere in flanking alluvium
alternatives_considered.reason: Sites 31 and 33 follow the hard-rock isotope pattern and have the lowest pMC
